biochemQuestions.stem: What does the Michaelis constant (Km) of an enzyme represent?
biochemQuestions.explanation: The substrate concentration at which the reaction runs at half its maximum velocity. It is an inverse measure of affinity — a LOW Km means the enzyme is saturated at low substrate concentrations, so it binds tightly. Vmax, by contrast, reflects how much enzyme is present and how fast it can turn over once saturated.

choices.text: The total amount of enzyme present
The substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity
The energy of activation of the reaction
The maximum reaction velocity achievable

biochemQuestions.stem: How does a competitive inhibitor alter an enzyme's kinetics?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It raises the apparent Km while leaving Vmax unchanged. Because it competes for the active site, adding enough substrate outcompetes it and full velocity is still reachable — which is exactly why it looks like reduced affinity rather than reduced capacity. A non-competitive inhibitor does the opposite: Vmax falls and Km is unaffected.

choices.text: Km rises, Vmax unchanged
Vmax falls, Km unchanged
Both Km and Vmax fall
Neither is affected

biochemQuestions.stem: Why do enzymes speed up reactions?
biochemQuestions.explanation: They lower the activation energy by stabilising the transition state. Note what they do NOT do: the equilibrium position and the overall free energy change are untouched, so an enzyme accelerates a reaction in both directions equally. A thermodynamically unfavourable reaction stays unfavourable no matter which enzyme is present.

choices.text: They make the overall free energy change more negative
They lower activation energy by stabilising the transition state
They supply energy directly to the reactants
They change the equilibrium position in favor of product

biochemQuestions.stem: What characterises an allosteric enzyme?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Regulation through binding at a site distinct from the active site, producing a conformational change and a sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic velocity curve. This is what allows a pathway's output to feed back on its own first committed step — the basis of nearly all metabolic control, and the reason such enzymes sit at pathway branch points.

choices.text: Complete independence from any regulation
An inability to bind cofactors
Regulation via a site separate from the active site, giving sigmoidal kinetics
Absolute irreversibility of catalysis

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the difference between a cofactor and a coenzyme?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Cofactor is the broader term for any non-protein helper an enzyme requires; coenzymes are the organic subset, most of them vitamin-derived. That derivation is why the clinical consequence of a vitamin deficiency is predictable: lose the vitamin and every enzyme depending on its coenzyme slows, which is why deficiency syndromes affect multiple systems at once.

choices.text: Coenzymes are the organic subset of cofactors, usually vitamin-derived
They are entirely unrelated concepts
Coenzymes are always metal ions
Cofactors are proteins and coenzymes are not

biochemQuestions.stem: Why is the rate-limiting step of a pathway the usual point of regulation?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Because it is the slowest step, so controlling it controls flux through the whole sequence — regulating a fast downstream step achieves little when the bottleneck is upstream. It is typically the first committed, irreversible step, which also means regulation happens before substrate has been spent on a pathway the cell no longer needs.

choices.text: It is always the final step of the pathway
It is the bottleneck, so controlling it controls flux through the whole pathway
It consumes no energy
It is the only reversible step

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Phosphofructokinase-1, converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. It is inhibited by ATP and citrate — signals that energy is plentiful — and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. That makes it the point at which the cell decides whether to burn glucose at all.

choices.text: Aldolase
Pyruvate kinase
Phosphofructokinase-1
Hexokinase

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the net ATP yield of anaerobic glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Two. Four ATP are produced but two are invested in the early phosphorylation steps. It is a small yield compared with the roughly thirty from complete oxidation, but it needs no oxygen and no mitochondria — which is why the red cell and exercising muscle depend on it.

choices.text: 38 ATP
2 ATP
12 ATP
0 ATP

biochemQuestions.stem: Why must pyruvate be converted to lactate when oxygen is scarce?
biochemQuestions.explanation: To regenerate NAD+. Glycolysis consumes NAD+ at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and without oxidative phosphorylation to recycle it the pathway would halt within seconds. Lactate dehydrogenase is therefore not a waste step but the mechanism that keeps anaerobic glycolysis running.

choices.text: To regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue
To synthesise glucose
To consume excess oxygen
To generate additional ATP directly

biochemQuestions.stem: How does hepatic glucokinase differ from hexokinase in other tissues?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Glucokinase has a high Km and is not inhibited by its product, so it only becomes active when portal glucose is high — after a meal. That makes the liver a glucose buffer rather than a competitor: it takes up glucose when there is plenty and leaves it for the brain when there is not.

choices.text: It is found only in muscle
Low Km, so it works at all glucose concentrations
High Km and no product inhibition, so it acts only when glucose is abundant
It phosphorylates fructose rather than glucose

biochemQuestions.stem: Why can fatty acids not be used for net glucose synthesis in humans?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Because the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate. Acetyl-CoA entering the TCA cycle loses two carbons as CO2, leaving no net carbon for gluconeogenesis. Glycerol from the triglyceride backbone and the odd-chain propionyl-CoA route are the exceptions, and neither is quantitatively significant.

choices.text: Fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria at all
Gluconeogenesis does not occur in humans
Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA cannot return to pyruvate
Fatty acid oxidation produces no usable intermediates

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the main function of the BUN cycle?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Converting ammonia — neurotoxic, especially to the central nervous system — into BUN for renal excretion. Defects at any step, or liver failure, cause hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy. This is why protein restriction and measures to reduce ammonia production are central to managing both inherited BUN cycle disorders and hepatic encephalopathy.

choices.text: Synthesising amino acids from glucose
Generating ATP for hepatocytes
Converting toxic ammonia into BUN for excretion
Producing ammonia from BUN

biochemQuestions.stem: Where and when are ketone bodies produced?
biochemQuestions.explanation: In liver mitochondria, when acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation exceeds the TCA cycle's capacity to process it — typically prolonged fasting, a very low carbohydrate intake, or insulin deficiency. The liver makes them but cannot use them, because it lacks the transferase needed; they are fuel exported for brain, heart and muscle.

choices.text: In muscle cytosol immediately after eating
In the brain, continuously
In adipose tissue during the fed state
In liver mitochondria, when acetyl-CoA exceeds TCA capacity

biochemQuestions.stem: What does lipoprotein lipase do, and where does it act?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It sits on capillary endothelium and hydrolyses triglycerides in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL, releasing fatty acids for uptake by muscle and adipose tissue. Deficiency causes severe hypertriglyceridaemia with milky plasma and a risk of pancreatitis, because the triglyceride-rich particles are never unloaded.

choices.text: Transports cholesterol from tissues back to the liver
Converts cholesterol to bile acids in the liver
Hydrolyses triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL at the capillary endothelium
Synthesises triglycerides inside adipocytes

biochemQuestions.stem: Why is HDL described as performing reverse cholesterol transport?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It collects cholesterol from peripheral tissues and returns it to the liver for excretion in bile — the opposite direction to LDL, which delivers cholesterol outward. This is the mechanistic basis for the epidemiological association between higher HDL and lower cardiovascular risk, though raising HDL pharmacologically has not reliably reproduced that benefit.

choices.text: It prevents all cholesterol absorption from the gut
It returns cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver
It delivers cholesterol from liver to tissues
It converts cholesterol into triglyceride

biochemQuestions.stem: Why are linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid described as essential fatty acids?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Humans lack the desaturases needed to introduce double bonds at those positions, so these fatty acids must come from the diet. They are precursors for longer-chain polyunsaturates and for eicosanoids, which is why prolonged fat-free feeding produces dermatitis and poor wound healing.

choices.text: They cannot be absorbed from the diet
Humans lack the desaturases to make them, so they must be eaten
They are the only fatty acids that yield ATP
They are synthesised only in the brain

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the purpose of transamination in amino acid metabolism?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Transferring an amino group to a keto acid, so the carbon skeleton can enter metabolism while nitrogen is funnelled towards disposal. The transaminases require pyridoxal phosphate from vitamin B6 — which is why B6 deficiency disturbs amino acid handling broadly, and why ALT and AST rise when hepatocytes are damaged.

choices.text: Converting glucose directly into protein
Breaking peptide bonds in dietary protein
Adding a carboxyl group to an amino acid
Transferring an amino group to a keto acid, separating nitrogen from carbon skeleton

biochemQuestions.stem: What distinguishes an essential from a non-essential amino acid?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised by the body and must be supplied by the diet. Some become 'conditionally essential' when synthesis fails or demand rises — tyrosine in phenylketonuria, for instance. This is why protein quality, not just quantity, determines nutritional adequacy.

choices.text: Essential ones are needed in larger absolute amounts
Non-essential ones have no metabolic role
Only essential amino acids can form peptide bonds
Essential ones cannot be synthesised and must come from the diet

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does denaturation abolish enzyme activity without breaking peptide bonds?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Because catalysis depends on the precise three-dimensional shape of the active site, and denaturation disrupts the non-covalent interactions holding that shape while leaving the amino acid sequence intact. Heat, extremes of pH and certain solutes all do this — the sequence survives, the function does not.

choices.text: Cofactors are chemically destroyed first
Peptide bonds are hydrolyzed by heat
The amino acid sequence is rearranged
The three-dimensional shape of the active site is lost while sequence remains

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis, and the target of statins?
biochemQuestions.explanation: HMG-CoA reductase. Inhibiting it lowers intracellular cholesterol, which upregulates hepatic LDL receptors — and it is that receptor upregulation, more than reduced synthesis itself, that clears LDL from the plasma. It also explains why statins work poorly in homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, where functional receptors are absent.

choices.text: HMG-CoA reductase
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
Lipoprotein lipase

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the role of carnitine in fatty acid oxidation?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It shuttles long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane, which they cannot cross as CoA esters. Carnitine deficiency therefore causes accumulation of long-chain fats with hypoketotic hypoglycemia and muscle weakness — the fat is available but cannot reach the site of oxidation.

choices.text: Synthesising cholesterol from acetyl-CoA
Emulsifying dietary fat in the gut
Activating fatty acids in the cytosol
Transporting long-chain fatty acyl groups into mitochondria

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme is deficient in classical phenylketonuria?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase, so phenylalanine accumulates and tyrosine becomes conditionally essential. Untreated it causes severe intellectual disability, which is entirely preventable by dietary restriction from birth — the reason it is on newborn screening programs worldwide. A minority of cases instead reflect defective tetrahydrobiopterin, the cofactor.

choices.text: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase
Cystathionine beta-synthase
Homogentisate oxidase
Phenylalanine hydroxylase

biochemQuestions.stem: What level of protein structure is stabilized primarily by hydrogen bonding within the backbone?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Secondary structure — the alpha helices and beta sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between backbone amide and carbonyl groups. Tertiary structure depends on side-chain interactions including hydrophobic packing and disulphide bridges, and quaternary on assembly of separate subunits.

choices.text: Tertiary structure
Quaternary structure
Primary structure
Secondary structure

biochemQuestions.stem: Which vitamin is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, and what happens when it is deficient?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Thiamine (B1), as thiamine pyrophosphate. Deficiency blocks entry of pyruvate into the TCA cycle, so lactate accumulates and ATP production falls — most damagingly in the brain and heart, giving Wernicke encephalopathy and wet beriberi. Glucose given before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's, which is why thiamine comes first in the at-risk patient.

choices.text: Thiamine — deficiency blocks pyruvate entry to the TCA cycle
Vitamin K — deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time
Vitamin C — deficiency causes bleeding gums only
Vitamin D — deficiency causes rickets

biochemQuestions.stem: What role does vitamin K play in coagulation?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It is the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on factors II, VII, IX and X, which is what lets those factors bind calcium and phospholipid surfaces. Warfarin blocks the recycling of vitamin K, which is why its effect takes days — existing carboxylated factors must first be cleared.

choices.text: Gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X
Breakdown of formed clots
Direct activation of platelets
Synthesis of fibrinogen from amino acids

biochemQuestions.stem: Both vitamin B12 and folate deficiency cause megaloblastic anemia. What distinguishes them biochemically?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Methylmalonic acid is raised in B12 deficiency but normal in folate deficiency, because B12 is additionally required by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Homocysteine rises in both. The distinction matters clinically: giving folate alone to someone B12-deficient corrects the anemia while the neurological damage continues.

choices.text: There is no biochemical difference
Methylmalonic acid is raised only in B12 deficiency
Only folate deficiency affects the blood film
Homocysteine rises only in folate deficiency

biochemQuestions.stem: Which vitamin is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Niacin (B3), which can also be made in limited amounts from tryptophan. Because NAD+ participates in a vast number of oxidation-reduction reactions, deficiency affects the tissues with the highest turnover — giving pellagra's dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia.

choices.text: Niacin
Biotin
Riboflavin
Pantothenic acid

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the principal function of the pentose phosphate pathway?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Producing NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate — reducing power for biosynthesis and antioxidant defense, and the sugar backbone for nucleotides. It generates no ATP. Its importance is clearest in the red cell, where NADPH maintains reduced glutathione, and where losing it causes oxidative hemolysis.

choices.text: Generating NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate
Synthesising fatty acids directly
Breaking down amino acids
Producing large amounts of ATP

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme deficiency causes von Gierke disease, with severe fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphatase. Without it the liver can neither release glucose from glycogen nor from gluconeogenesis, so glucose-6-phosphate accumulates and no glucose reaches the circulation. That explains the combination of a large glycogen-loaded liver alongside profound hypoglycemia — the fuel is present but cannot leave the cell.

choices.text: Branching enzyme
Lysosomal acid maltase
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Muscle glycogen phosphorylase

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does vitamin C deficiency weaken connective tissue?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Ascorbate is required for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen, and without it the triple helix cannot cross-link properly. The resulting fragile collagen explains scurvy's picture: bleeding gums, poor wound healing, perifollicular hemorrhage and loose teeth.

choices.text: Elastin replaces collagen entirely
Calcium cannot be absorbed at all
Collagen genes are mutated by the deficiency
Collagen proline and lysine hydroxylation fails, so cross-linking is defective

biochemQuestions.stem: What does semiconservative DNA replication mean?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Each daughter molecule retains one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand. The parental strand acts as the template, which is what makes replication accurate and allows mismatch repair to identify which strand is new — and therefore which base is the error.

choices.text: Each new molecule keeps one parental and one new strand
Both strands of each new molecule are newly made
The original molecule is destroyed and rebuilt
Only one strand is ever copied

biochemQuestions.stem: In which direction does DNA polymerase synthesise a new strand?
biochemQuestions.explanation: 5′ to 3′ only, adding nucleotides to the free 3′ hydroxyl. This single constraint explains the whole architecture of the replication fork: one strand is copied continuously while the other must be made in short segments and joined, and it is why a primer is always required.

choices.text: Either direction, depending on the template
From the middle of the strand outwards

biochemQuestions.stem: What is meant by the degeneracy of the genetic code?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Several codons can specify the same amino acid, most often differing at the third base. This is why many single-base substitutions are silent and have no effect on the protein, and it provides a genuine buffer against mutation rather than being a quirk of the code.

choices.text: The code differs between human tissues
One codon can code for several different amino acids
Several codons can code for the same amino acid
Some codons code for nothing at all

biochemQuestions.stem: Why is a frameshift mutation usually more damaging than a missense mutation?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Inserting or deleting a number of bases not divisible by three shifts the reading frame, so every downstream codon is misread and a premature stop is likely. A missense mutation changes one amino acid; a frameshift typically destroys the entire remainder of the protein.

choices.text: It only affects the first amino acid
The reading frame shifts, so all downstream codons are misread
It prevents transcription from starting
It always deletes the whole gene

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the purpose of splicing in eukaryotic gene expression?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Removing introns and joining exons to produce mature mRNA. Alternative splicing lets one gene generate several proteins, which is part of why the human protein repertoire greatly exceeds the gene count. Mutations at splice sites can be as damaging as those in coding sequence.

choices.text: Translating mRNA into protein
Adding introns to increase protein diversity
Copying DNA into a complementary strand
Removing introns and joining exons to form mature mRNA

biochemQuestions.stem: What does the polymerase chain reaction achieve?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Exponential amplification of a specific DNA sequence defined by the primers, through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. Because amplification is exponential, tiny starting amounts become detectable — which is the basis of molecular diagnostics and also why contamination causes false positives.

choices.text: Translation of RNA into protein in vitro
Separation of proteins by size
Direct sequencing of a whole genome in one step
Exponential amplification of a specific DNA sequence

biochemQuestions.stem: A Western blot detects which type of molecule?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Protein, using antibodies after electrophoretic separation. Southern blotting detects DNA and Northern detects RNA — a distinction worth fixing, because the choice of technique reveals what question is being asked of the sample.

choices.text: Carbohydrate
Protein
DNA
RNA

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme is deficient in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, the purine salvage enzyme. Losing salvage forces reliance on de novo synthesis and diverts purines to uric acid, giving hyperuricaemia with gout and renal stones alongside the neurological features. It is X-linked recessive.

choices.text: Adenosine deaminase
Xanthine oxidase
Dihydrofolate reductase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT)

biochemQuestions.stem: How does allopurinol lower uric acid?
biochemQuestions.explanation: By inhibiting xanthine oxidase, so hypoxanthine and xanthine are not converted to uric acid. Those precursors are more soluble and more readily excreted. It is prophylactic rather than a treatment for acute gout — starting it during an attack can prolong it.

choices.text: It increases renal uric acid reabsorption
It converts uric acid into purines
It inhibits xanthine oxidase
It blocks purine absorption from the diet

biochemQuestions.stem: How does methotrexate interfere with nucleotide synthesis?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate and so blocking thymidine and purine synthesis. Rapidly dividing cells suffer first, which accounts for both the antineoplastic effect and the toxicity to marrow and gut mucosa. Folinic acid rescue bypasses the blocked step.

choices.text: It inhibits xanthine oxidase
It cross-links DNA strands directly
It blocks the ribosome
It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does adenosine deaminase deficiency cause severe combined immunodeficiency?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Deoxyadenosine and its nucleotides accumulate and are particularly toxic to lymphocytes, which cannot tolerate the resulting imbalance in deoxynucleotide pools. Both T and B cell lineages fail, hence the combined defect — and it was the first condition treated by gene therapy.

choices.text: Antibodies are structurally abnormal
The thymus is absent from birth
Toxic deoxyadenosine metabolites accumulate and destroy lymphocytes
Complement proteins are not synthesised

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme does 5-fluorouracil inhibit?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Thymidylate synthase, so dTMP cannot be made and DNA synthesis stalls. As with methotrexate the effect falls hardest on rapidly dividing tissue, explaining the characteristic mucositis, diarrhea and myelosuppression.

choices.text: Ribonucleotide reductase
Thymidylate synthase
DNA ligase
Topoisomerase II

biochemQuestions.stem: What does the chemiosmotic theory propose about ATP synthesis?
biochemQuestions.explanation: That electron transport pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, and the resulting electrochemical gradient drives ATP synthase as protons flow back. The gradient — not a chemical intermediate — is the stored energy, which is why anything that makes the membrane leaky abolishes ATP synthesis while electron transport continues.

choices.text: A proton gradient across the inner membrane drives ATP synthase
ATP is made directly by the electron transport complexes
Substrate-level phosphorylation supplies all mitochondrial ATP
Oxygen is not required at any stage

biochemQuestions.stem: How does an uncoupling agent such as 2,4-dinitrophenol affect mitochondria?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It carries protons across the membrane, dissipating the gradient. Electron transport and oxygen consumption accelerate while ATP synthesis falls, and the energy appears as heat — which is why uncouplers cause dangerous hyperthermia. Brown adipose tissue uses the same principle physiologically via thermogenin.

choices.text: It prevents oxygen consumption entirely
It blocks electron transport completely
It dissipates the proton gradient, so energy is released as heat instead of ATP
It increases ATP yield per glucose molecule

biochemQuestions.stem: Where does cyanide act in oxidative phosphorylation?
biochemQuestions.explanation: At complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, blocking the transfer of electrons to oxygen. Cells cannot use oxygen even though it is delivered normally, so venous oxygen content stays high and lactate rises steeply. That mismatch — adequate oxygenation with profound lactic acidosis — is the diagnostic clue.

choices.text: The carnitine shuttle
Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase
ATP synthase
Complex I only

biochemQuestions.stem: What does a respiratory quotient of approximately 1.0 indicate about substrate use?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Predominantly carbohydrate oxidation, because glucose oxidation produces roughly one molecule of CO2 per molecule of O2 consumed. Fat oxidation gives a lower value near 0.7, since fatty acids are more reduced and need proportionally more oxygen — so the ratio reports which fuel is being burnt.

choices.text: Mainly carbohydrate oxidation
No metabolism is occurring
Mainly fat oxidation
Mainly protein oxidation

biochemQuestions.stem: Which fuel does the brain use during prolonged starvation, and why does that matter?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It shifts substantially to ketone bodies. This spares glucose and therefore spares muscle protein, since gluconeogenesis would otherwise consume amino acids. The adaptation is what allows survival for weeks rather than days — the brain cannot use fatty acids directly, so ketones are the only alternative.

choices.text: Only glucose, in all circumstances
Ketone bodies, which spare glucose and therefore muscle protein
Lactate exclusively
Fatty acids taken up directly across the blood-brain barrier

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does insulin deficiency cause ketoacidosis?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Unopposed lipolysis floods the liver with fatty acids, and their oxidation generates acetyl-CoA far in excess of TCA capacity, so ketone bodies accumulate as acids. Glucose is abundant in the blood but cannot enter cells, so the body behaves as though starving — starvation in the midst of plenty.

choices.text: The kidneys stop excreting all acid
Unrestrained lipolysis floods the liver with fatty acids, overwhelming TCA capacity
Excess glucose is directly converted into acid
Protein synthesis produces acidic by-products

biochemQuestions.stem: What does glucagon do to hepatic metabolism during fasting?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and promotes ketogenesis, raising blood glucose. It acts principally on the liver, since muscle lacks glucagon receptors — which is why muscle glycogen cannot contribute directly to blood glucose and must go through the Cori cycle instead.

choices.text: Lowers blood glucose
Stimulates glycogen synthesis in muscle
Stimulates glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis, mainly in liver
Promotes glucose uptake into adipose tissue

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does the liver, not muscle, regulate blood glucose despite muscle holding more glycogen?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot release free glucose into the circulation — its glycogen serves only the muscle itself. The liver has the enzyme, and so is the only tissue that can export stored glucose to the rest of the body.

choices.text: Muscle glycogen is inaccessible to any enzyme
Muscle has no glycogen phosphorylase
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot export free glucose
Muscle glycogen is chemically different

biochemQuestions.stem: Why is newborn screening for metabolic disease worth doing?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Because several of these conditions cause irreversible damage before symptoms appear, and dietary or pharmacological treatment started presymptomatically prevents it almost entirely. Phenylketonuria is the model case: detected at birth the outcome is normal, detected on symptoms the damage is permanent.

choices.text: Damage is irreversible but preventable if treatment starts before symptoms
It replaces the need for any family history
The conditions are untreatable but worth documenting
The conditions only appear in adulthood

biochemQuestions.stem: Why is maple syrup urine disease a metabolic emergency in the newborn?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency lets leucine and its ketoacid accumulate to neurotoxic levels within days, causing encephalopathy and death if untreated. Management is urgent removal of the accumulated metabolites and restriction of branched-chain amino acid intake — a delay of hours matters.

choices.text: Branched-chain amino acids accumulate rapidly to neurotoxic levels
It causes gradual liver fibrosis over years
It affects skin pigmentation alone
It presents only in adolescence

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does the red blood cell depend entirely on glycolysis for ATP?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It has no mitochondria, so oxidative phosphorylation is unavailable despite the cell being full of oxygen. Its energy needs are met by anaerobic glycolysis alone, which is why glycolytic enzyme defects such as pyruvate kinase deficiency present as hemolytic anemia.

choices.text: It has no mitochondria
It cannot take up glucose
It lacks all glycolytic enzymes
Oxygen is toxic to its enzymes

biochemQuestions.stem: What are insulin's principal metabolic effects after a meal?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It promotes storage: glucose uptake into muscle and adipose tissue, glycogen and triglyceride synthesis, and protein synthesis, while suppressing gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and lipolysis. Every one of those actions is anabolic, which is why insulin deficiency produces simultaneous hyperglycemia, ketosis and wasting.

choices.text: It raises blood glucose
It promotes storage and suppresses gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and lipolysis
It acts only on the liver
It stimulates glycogen breakdown and lipolysis

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the Cori cycle?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in muscle travels to the liver, is converted back to glucose by gluconeogenesis, and returns to muscle. The liver bears the ATP cost so muscle can keep contracting — an inter-organ division of labor rather than a futile loop.

choices.text: Muscle lactate is converted to glucose in the liver and returned to muscle
Muscle glucose is converted to fat in adipose tissue
Liver ketones are converted to glucose in the brain
Amino acids are converted to BUN in muscle

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does G6PD deficiency cause hemolysis on oxidative stress?
biochemQuestions.explanation: The pentose phosphate pathway cannot generate enough NADPH to keep glutathione reduced, so hemoglobin oxidises and precipitates as Heinz bodies and the red cell membrane is damaged. Infections, fava beans and certain drugs precipitate it — and the red cell is uniquely vulnerable because it has no alternative NADPH source.

choices.text: Insufficient NADPH to maintain reduced glutathione
Failure of hemoglobin synthesis
Absent glycolytic enzymes
An abnormal beta-globin chain

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the biochemical problem in classical galactosaemia?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates and is toxic to liver, brain and lens. Removing lactose and galactose from the diet prevents the acute crisis, which is why it must be recognized in the first days of life.

choices.text: Inability to absorb any dietary sugar
Deficiency of lactase in the gut only
Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, with toxic accumulation
Excess galactose synthesis by the liver

biochemQuestions.stem: What underlies the lysosomal storage disorders as a group?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Deficiency of a lysosomal hydrolase, so its substrate accumulates progressively inside lysosomes and the cell enlarges and fails. Which substrate accumulates determines which organs suffer — hence the very different pictures of Gaucher, Tay-Sachs and Fabry disease despite a shared underlying mechanism.

choices.text: Overproduction of lysosomal enzymes
Failure of mitochondrial replication
Absence of lysosomes altogether
A deficient lysosomal enzyme, so its substrate accumulates progressively

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does mitochondrial disease show maternal inheritance?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost entirely from the oocyte, so an affected mother can transmit to all her children while an affected father transmits to none. Variable heteroplasmy — the proportion of mutant mitochondria differing between tissues and between siblings — explains why severity varies so widely within one family.

choices.text: Paternal mitochondria replicate faster
Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the oocyte
Mitochondria contain no DNA of their own
The genes involved are all X-linked

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the metabolic role of the TCA cycle beyond energy production?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It supplies intermediates for biosynthesis — oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis and aspartate, alpha-ketoglutarate for glutamate, succinyl-CoA for heme. Because intermediates are withdrawn, they must be replenished by anaplerotic reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase, or the cycle grinds down.

choices.text: It provides biosynthetic intermediates, replenished by anaplerotic reactions
It synthesises fatty acids directly
It operates only under anaerobic conditions
It has no function other than making ATP

biochemQuestions.stem: What does the Michaelis constant (Km) of an enzyme represent?
biochemQuestions.explanation: The substrate concentration at which the reaction runs at half its maximum velocity. It is an inverse measure of affinity — a LOW Km means the enzyme is saturated at low substrate concentrations, so it binds tightly. Vmax, by contrast, reflects how much enzyme is present and how fast it can turn over once saturated.

choices.text: The energy of activation of the reaction
The maximum reaction velocity achievable

Homocysteine rises in both. The distinction matters clinically: giving folate alone to someone B12-deficient corrects the anemia while the neurological damage continues.

choices.text: Methylmalonic acid is raised only in B12 deficiency
Only folate deficiency affects the blood film
There is no biochemical difference
Homocysteine rises only in folate deficiency

biochemQuestions.stem: Which vitamin is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Niacin (B3), which can also be made in limited amounts from tryptophan. Because NAD+ participates in a vast number of oxidation-reduction reactions, deficiency affects the tissues with the highest turnover — giving pellagra's dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia.

choices.text: Niacin
Pantothenic acid
Biotin
Riboflavin

biochemQuestions.stem: Why is a frameshift mutation usually more damaging than a missense mutation?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Inserting or deleting a number of bases not divisible by three shifts the reading frame, so every downstream codon is misread and a premature stop is likely. A missense mutation changes one amino acid; a frameshift typically destroys the entire remainder of the protein.

choices.text: The reading frame shifts, so all downstream codons are misread
It always deletes the whole gene
It prevents transcription from starting
It only affects the first amino acid

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the purpose of splicing in eukaryotic gene expression?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Removing introns and joining exons to produce mature mRNA. Alternative splicing lets one gene generate several proteins, which is part of why the human protein repertoire greatly exceeds the gene count. Mutations at splice sites can be as damaging as those in coding sequence.

choices.text: Copying DNA into a complementary strand
Translating mRNA into protein
Removing introns and joining exons to form mature mRNA
Adding introns to increase protein diversity

biochemQuestions.stem: What does the polymerase chain reaction achieve?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Exponential amplification of a specific DNA sequence defined by the primers, through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. Because amplification is exponential, tiny starting amounts become detectable — which is the basis of molecular diagnostics and also why contamination causes false positives.

choices.text: Translation of RNA into protein in vitro
Direct sequencing of a whole genome in one step
Exponential amplification of a specific DNA sequence
Separation of proteins by size

biochemQuestions.stem: A Western blot detects which type of molecule?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Protein, using antibodies after electrophoretic separation. Southern blotting detects DNA and Northern detects RNA — a distinction worth fixing, because the choice of technique reveals what question is being asked of the sample.

choices.text: Carbohydrate
RNA
Protein
DNA

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme is deficient in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, the purine salvage enzyme. Losing salvage forces reliance on de novo synthesis and diverts purines to uric acid, giving hyperuricaemia with gout and renal stones alongside the neurological features. It is X-linked recessive.

choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase
Adenosine deaminase
Xanthine oxidase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT)

biochemQuestions.stem: How does allopurinol lower uric acid?
biochemQuestions.explanation: By inhibiting xanthine oxidase, so hypoxanthine and xanthine are not converted to uric acid. Those precursors are more soluble and more readily excreted. It is prophylactic rather than a treatment for acute gout — starting it during an attack can prolong it.

choices.text: It inhibits xanthine oxidase
It blocks purine absorption from the diet
It converts uric acid into purines
It increases renal uric acid reabsorption

biochemQuestions.stem: How does methotrexate interfere with nucleotide synthesis?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate and so blocking thymidine and purine synthesis. Rapidly dividing cells suffer first, which accounts for both the antineoplastic effect and the toxicity to marrow and gut mucosa. Folinic acid rescue bypasses the blocked step.

choices.text: It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate
It cross-links DNA strands directly
It inhibits xanthine oxidase
It blocks the ribosome

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does adenosine deaminase deficiency cause severe combined immunodeficiency?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Deoxyadenosine and its nucleotides accumulate and are particularly toxic to lymphocytes, which cannot tolerate the resulting imbalance in deoxynucleotide pools. Both T and B cell lineages fail, hence the combined defect — and it was the first condition treated by gene therapy.

choices.text: Toxic deoxyadenosine metabolites accumulate and destroy lymphocytes
Complement proteins are not synthesised
Antibodies are structurally abnormal
The thymus is absent from birth

biochemQuestions.stem: What does the chemiosmotic theory propose about ATP synthesis?
biochemQuestions.explanation: That electron transport pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, and the resulting electrochemical gradient drives ATP synthase as protons flow back. The gradient — not a chemical intermediate — is the stored energy, which is why anything that makes the membrane leaky abolishes ATP synthesis while electron transport continues.

choices.text: A proton gradient across the inner membrane drives ATP synthase
ATP is made directly by the electron transport complexes
Oxygen is not required at any stage
Substrate-level phosphorylation supplies all mitochondrial ATP

biochemQuestions.stem: How does an uncoupling agent such as 2,4-dinitrophenol affect mitochondria?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It carries protons across the membrane, dissipating the gradient. Electron transport and oxygen consumption accelerate while ATP synthesis falls, and the energy appears as heat — which is why uncouplers cause dangerous hyperthermia. Brown adipose tissue uses the same principle physiologically via thermogenin.

choices.text: It increases ATP yield per glucose molecule
It dissipates the proton gradient, so energy is released as heat instead of ATP
It blocks electron transport completely
It prevents oxygen consumption entirely

biochemQuestions.stem: Where does cyanide act in oxidative phosphorylation?
biochemQuestions.explanation: At complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, blocking the transfer of electrons to oxygen. Cells cannot use oxygen even though it is delivered normally, so venous oxygen content stays high and lactate rises steeply. That mismatch — adequate oxygenation with profound lactic acidosis — is the diagnostic clue.

choices.text: The carnitine shuttle
ATP synthase
Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase
Complex I only

biochemQuestions.stem: What does a respiratory quotient of approximately 1.0 indicate about substrate use?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Predominantly carbohydrate oxidation, because glucose oxidation produces roughly one molecule of CO2 per molecule of O2 consumed. Fat oxidation gives a lower value near 0.7, since fatty acids are more reduced and need proportionally more oxygen — so the ratio reports which fuel is being burnt.

choices.text: Mainly carbohydrate oxidation
Mainly fat oxidation
Mainly protein oxidation
No metabolism is occurring

biochemQuestions.stem: Which fuel does the brain use during prolonged starvation, and why does that matter?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It shifts substantially to ketone bodies. This spares glucose and therefore spares muscle protein, since gluconeogenesis would otherwise consume amino acids. The adaptation is what allows survival for weeks rather than days — the brain cannot use fatty acids directly, so ketones are the only alternative.

choices.text: Lactate exclusively
Ketone bodies, which spare glucose and therefore muscle protein
Fatty acids taken up directly across the blood-brain barrier
Only glucose, in all circumstances

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the metabolic role of the TCA cycle beyond energy production?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It supplies intermediates for biosynthesis — oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis and aspartate, alpha-ketoglutarate for glutamate, succinyl-CoA for heme. Because intermediates are withdrawn, they must be replenished by anaplerotic reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase, or the cycle grinds down.

choices.text: It operates only under anaerobic conditions
It has no function other than making ATP
It provides biosynthetic intermediates, replenished by anaplerotic reactions
It synthesises fatty acids directly

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does the red blood cell depend entirely on glycolysis for ATP?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It has no mitochondria, so oxidative phosphorylation is unavailable despite the cell being full of oxygen. Its energy needs are met by anaerobic glycolysis alone, which is why glycolytic enzyme defects such as pyruvate kinase deficiency present as hemolytic anemia.

choices.text: It lacks all glycolytic enzymes
It has no mitochondria
It cannot take up glucose
Oxygen is toxic to its enzymes

biochemQuestions.stem: What are insulin's principal metabolic effects after a meal?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It promotes storage: glucose uptake into muscle and adipose tissue, glycogen and triglyceride synthesis, and protein synthesis, while suppressing gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and lipolysis. Every one of those actions is anabolic, which is why insulin deficiency produces simultaneous hyperglycemia, ketosis and wasting.

choices.text: It acts only on the liver
It raises blood glucose
It stimulates glycogen breakdown and lipolysis
It promotes storage and suppresses gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and lipolysis

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does insulin deficiency cause ketoacidosis?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Unopposed lipolysis floods the liver with fatty acids, and their oxidation generates acetyl-CoA far in excess of TCA capacity, so ketone bodies accumulate as acids. Glucose is abundant in the blood but cannot enter cells, so the body behaves as though starving — starvation in the midst of plenty.

choices.text: The kidneys stop excreting all acid
Unrestrained lipolysis floods the liver with fatty acids, overwhelming TCA capacity
Protein synthesis produces acidic by-products
Excess glucose is directly converted into acid

biochemQuestions.stem: What does glucagon do to hepatic metabolism during fasting?
biochemQuestions.explanation: It stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and promotes ketogenesis, raising blood glucose. It acts principally on the liver, since muscle lacks glucagon receptors — which is why muscle glycogen cannot contribute directly to blood glucose and must go through the Cori cycle instead.

choices.text: Stimulates glycogen synthesis in muscle
Lowers blood glucose
Promotes glucose uptake into adipose tissue
Stimulates glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis, mainly in liver

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does the liver, not muscle, regulate blood glucose despite muscle holding more glycogen?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot release free glucose into the circulation — its glycogen serves only the muscle itself. The liver has the enzyme, and so is the only tissue that can export stored glucose to the rest of the body.

choices.text: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot export free glucose
Muscle has no glycogen phosphorylase
Muscle glycogen is chemically different
Muscle glycogen is inaccessible to any enzyme

biochemQuestions.stem: Why is newborn screening for metabolic disease worth doing?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Because several of these conditions cause irreversible damage before symptoms appear, and dietary or pharmacological treatment started presymptomatically prevents it almost entirely. Phenylketonuria is the model case: detected at birth the outcome is normal, detected on symptoms the damage is permanent.

choices.text: Damage is irreversible but preventable if treatment starts before symptoms
The conditions are untreatable but worth documenting
The conditions only appear in adulthood
It replaces the need for any family history

biochemQuestions.stem: Why is maple syrup urine disease a metabolic emergency in the newborn?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency lets leucine and its ketoacid accumulate to neurotoxic levels within days, causing encephalopathy and death if untreated. Management is urgent removal of the accumulated metabolites and restriction of branched-chain amino acid intake — a delay of hours matters.

choices.text: It affects skin pigmentation alone
It presents only in adolescence
Branched-chain amino acids accumulate rapidly to neurotoxic levels
It causes gradual liver fibrosis over years

biochemQuestions.stem: What underlies the lysosomal storage disorders as a group?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Deficiency of a lysosomal hydrolase, so its substrate accumulates progressively inside lysosomes and the cell enlarges and fails. Which substrate accumulates determines which organs suffer — hence the very different pictures of Gaucher, Tay-Sachs and Fabry disease despite a shared underlying mechanism.

choices.text: A deficient lysosomal enzyme, so its substrate accumulates progressively
Failure of mitochondrial replication
Absence of lysosomes altogether
Overproduction of lysosomal enzymes

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does mitochondrial disease show maternal inheritance?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost entirely from the oocyte, so an affected mother can transmit to all her children while an affected father transmits to none. Variable heteroplasmy — the proportion of mutant mitochondria differing between tissues and between siblings — explains why severity varies so widely within one family.

choices.text: Paternal mitochondria replicate faster
Mitochondria contain no DNA of their own
Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the oocyte
The genes involved are all X-linked

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the biochemical problem in classical galactosaemia?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates and is toxic to liver, brain and lens. Removing lactose and galactose from the diet prevents the acute crisis, which is why it must be recognized in the first days of life.

choices.text: Excess galactose synthesis by the liver
Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, with toxic accumulation
Inability to absorb any dietary sugar
Deficiency of lactase in the gut only

biochemQuestions.stem: What is the principal function of the pentose phosphate pathway?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Producing NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate — reducing power for biosynthesis and antioxidant defense, and the sugar backbone for nucleotides. It generates no ATP. Its importance is clearest in the red cell, where NADPH maintains reduced glutathione, and where losing it causes oxidative hemolysis.

choices.text: Breaking down amino acids
Producing large amounts of ATP
Synthesising fatty acids directly
Generating NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme deficiency causes von Gierke disease, with severe fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphatase. Without it the liver can neither release glucose from glycogen nor from gluconeogenesis, so glucose-6-phosphate accumulates and no glucose reaches the circulation. That explains the combination of a large glycogen-loaded liver alongside profound hypoglycemia — the fuel is present but cannot leave the cell.

choices.text: Branching enzyme
Muscle glycogen phosphorylase
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Lysosomal acid maltase

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme is deficient in classical phenylketonuria?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase, so phenylalanine accumulates and tyrosine becomes conditionally essential. Untreated it causes severe intellectual disability, which is entirely preventable by dietary restriction from birth — the reason it is on newborn screening programs worldwide. A minority of cases instead reflect defective tetrahydrobiopterin, the cofactor.

choices.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase
Cystathionine beta-synthase
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase
Homogentisate oxidase

biochemQuestions.stem: Which enzyme does 5-fluorouracil inhibit?
biochemQuestions.explanation: Thymidylate synthase, so dTMP cannot be made and DNA synthesis stalls. As with methotrexate the effect falls hardest on rapidly dividing tissue, explaining the characteristic mucositis, diarrhea and myelosuppression.

choices.text: Ribonucleotide reductase
Topoisomerase II
DNA ligase
Thymidylate synthase

biochemQuestions.stem: Why does G6PD deficiency cause hemolysis on oxidative stress?
biochemQuestions.explanation: The pentose phosphate pathway cannot generate enough NADPH to keep glutathione reduced, so hemoglobin oxidises and precipitates as Heinz bodies and the red cell membrane is damaged. Infections, fava beans and certain drugs precipitate it — and the red cell is uniquely vulnerable because it has no alternative NADPH source.

choices.text: Insufficient NADPH to maintain reduced glutathione
An abnormal beta-globin chain
Failure of hemoglobin synthesis
Absent glycolytic enzymes
